* * *

EXAMPLE 6

Dramatic design
Viewpoint and approach (20%): Close third through Mara, twenty-two, an infrastructure-security engineer, arriving alone at Fulcrum's beautiful redwood-and-glass Northern California compound for the first time.
Concrete status transaction (45%): Outside at the evening welcome, a young fellow leaves a half-full glass on a low wall while continuing an important conversation. An older catering worker retrieves it without acknowledgment. Mara notices who assumes whose labor and makes one dry, specific inference.
Institutional turn (25%): Only after the transaction, polished founder Adrian welcomes Mara and makes her live observation the opening of a nonverbal calibration game.

Manuscript
When the last car in Mara’s small group of interviewees arrived, and when all the new recruits had received their badges, they were escorted in a single, quiet caravan from the front desk to the main building.
The new building’s interior was nearly as spectacular as the exterior. A high glass atrium overlooked the main entrance, and even on that bright afternoon, warm sunlight poured in, and illuminated the tall, slim palm trees standing in neat rows on the ground floor.
A long walkway bridged the upper floors, making them into a single open space. Employees were moving quietly to and fro. The sound of typing, phone conversations, and the hum of several hundred people talking softly was muted by the high, white ceilings and glass walls.
Mara did not know what she was looking at or who anybody was. A lot of people were wearing headphones, which made it look like a library. But there were no books anywhere. Everybody was dressed in clothes that looked like regular jeans and t-shirts and hoodies. Only the most eagle-eyed might note that all the hoodies were uniform dark-gray Fulcrum-branded sweats.
The woman who had checked Mara in followed the procession to an enormous table set with a few laptops.
“These are your computers, and this is where you’re going to plug in. You already know how to do that, right?”
The young men chuckled. Mara nodded.

Mara entered Fulcrum’s visitor parking lot through an automatic gate set far back on a narrow mountain road. The sign at the gate identified the company as “Fulcrum Technologies, LLC,” but she had yet to find a Fulcrum employee who used the word “technology” for what the company made. The word was old and associated with things that worked—machines that had replaceable parts. It wasn’t a good fit for Fulcrum.

At the gate Mara had shown her ID to a gray-haired, ruddy, bearded man in a leather cap who had looked at the ID but not at her face and seemed to know what he was supposed to be doing even though she had no idea how he fit in. Was he security? Did the company have some sort of formal visitor identification protocol? But the gate didn’t have an intercom and hadn’t seemed to be under any kind of video surveillance, and once Mara had entered, the lot was empty except for a few scattered bikes, and it had taken her a minute or two to find a spot where the tires of her rental wouldn’t sink into grass.

Her manager at work, John, who’d hired her right out of grad school, had said the parking lot would be empty because Fulcrum was “all about bicycles,” which was one reason he’d advised her against renting a car. He hadn’t said anything about security, but that was part of the Fulcrum myth: There was no security.

She carried her backpack to the only building she could see and went up some broad wooden stairs to a deck that faced north, with a view of redwood trees against a blue-and-cloudy sky. At the far end of the deck was an open sliding glass door that led into an empty hallway and beyond it, another hallway, lined on one side with office doors that were either slightly or very open. She hesitated, but there was no sign or doorbell or any indication that anyone was supposed to be there, so she went through the second hallway, feeling embarrassed about walking through the open doorways of strangers. At the end of the second hallway she entered a space that was neither a room nor a corridor: A row of wooden bookshelves on one side separated it from the next room, while the other side was entirely glass and looked out onto what might have been either a garden or just a wilderness of weeds—it had a pond but no visible plants.
